safekb-mcp — SafeKB local MCP client (stdio)

Usage:
  safekb-mcp --setup [--url <api url>] [--config <path>]
  safekb-mcp --mcp [--url <api url>] [--config <path>] [--keyring <dir>] [--sealed-only]
  safekb-mcp --authorize [--url <api url>] [--config <path>]
  safekb-mcp --configure [--config <path>]
  safekb-mcp --sidecar [--confirm] [--config <path>]
  safekb-mcp --export-keys <file> [--config <path>] [--keyring <dir>]
  safekb-mcp --import-keys <file> [--config <path>] [--keyring <dir>]
  safekb-mcp --list-keys [--config <path>] [--keyring <dir>]
  safekb-mcp --create-key <name> --space <space id> [--store system|file]
  safekb-mcp --rename-key <name or id> --name <new name>
  safekb-mcp --rotate-key <name or id> [--store system|file]
  safekb-mcp --move-key <name or id> --store system|file
  safekb-mcp --delete-key <name or id>
  safekb-mcp --auto-unlock <name or id>|all --set on|off
  safekb-mcp --export <file> [--space <space id>]... [--doc <document id>]... [--compress]
                     [--skip-locked]
  safekb-mcp --import <file> [--into-space <space id>] [--store system|file]
                     [--keys <key export>]...

Without arguments this text is printed.

Options:
  --mcp              Start the MCP server on stdio. This is what an MCP client is given as its
                     command.
  --setup            Everything in one step: authorize this computer in the browser, choose where
                     sealed keys are kept, and register the server with Claude Code. What is
                     already done is left as it is, so it can be run again.
  --url <api url>    SafeKB API base URL. Also: KB_API_URL. Otherwise the URL in the token file,
                     or https://api.safekb.com when authorizing.
                     When serving it must have the origin the token was issued for.
  --config <path>    Token file. Also: SAFEKB_MCP_CONFIG. Default: ~/.config/safekb/mcp.json
  --keyring <dir>    Directory of sealed key files. Also: SAFEKB_SEALED_KEYRING. Otherwise the one
                     in the store settings, if any.
  --sealed-only      Expose only the sealed tools; do not proxy the hosted tools.
  --authorize        Authorize this client again in the browser and replace the token file.
  --configure        Choose again where new sealed keys are kept: the system keyring, or key
                     files when this machine has none.
  --sidecar          Hold seal root secrets you type, in memory only and for a limited time, and
                     hand them to the client. Runs in its own terminal.
  --confirm          With --sidecar: ask before every release of a secret.
  --export-keys <file>  Write every sealed key this machine keeps (system keyring and key files) to
                     a new file, encrypted under a passphrase you type. Needs a terminal.
  --import-keys <file>  Read such a file and keep its keys in this machine's default store. A
                     key this machine already keeps is left as it is. Needs a terminal.
  --list-keys        Print every sealed key this machine keeps (system keyring and key files), one
                     per line: its store, its seal root (by name where this machine knows one),
                     its key id, and whether the server still has that key as the root's current
                     one. Never prints a key. Secrets held by the sidecar are in memory only and
                     are not listed.
  --create-key <name>  Create a sealed folder of that name at the top of the space given by
                     --space, as a new seal root with a generated key. The key is kept in the
                     store given by --store, or in the default store. Prints name, id and store.
  --rename-key <ref> Rename a seal root to the name given by --name: its sealed title on the
                     server and the name this machine knows it by. Needs its key in a local store.
  --rotate-key <ref> Replace the secret of a seal root with a newly generated key
